09196b5a433f: Appendix A · cadastral numbers, ownership and use of the name
d1aa43759628: Chapter 1 tells the story of the place, and chapter 6 how the name became the family’s. Here is the documentation: the cadastral numbers, the deeds and the place designations that do not fit together without further thought. The property can be followed document by document in the land registers and the deed and mortgage books; the use of names around it demands more patience. First the two kinds of source that seem to pull in different directions:
bc6ea85a3d8f: The parish-register entries consistently say <t1>Økjær</t1> when they give a place of residence. Thomas Jensen was a smallholder and fisherman in Økjær. Niels Thomsen was a smallholder and fisherman in Økjær. The children were born in Økjær. The censuses say something else: they list the household in <t2>Øe</t2> — and from 1890 with a cadastral number, <t3>13b</t3>, the number on which Silkjær lies today.
65507d420f5a: The otherwise obvious conclusion — that the family lived at Øhusevej 3 and merely borrowed the name from the neighbouring farm — does not hold up against the sources. Three censuses, <t1>1890, 1901 and 1911</t1>, place the household directly on cad. no. 13b in Øe — a span of twenty-one years. The census of 1880 lists Niels Thomsen in Øe, but without a cadastral number; the land register shows, however, that he had already obtained title to 13b in January 1879. Further back the lists are silent on the cadastral number: 1855, 1860 and 1870 have Thomas Jensen in Øe, but the older censuses do not give cadastral numbers. [S60, S61]
df532d803705: So much for the censuses. The court books put dates on the chain from chapter 1: the Ministry of the Interior’s resolution of 24 May 1851 on the division of parcel no. 2 from cad. no. 13; a deed of 19 June 1851 from Jens Thomsen — written in the deed as “af Øe Bye” (of Øe village), with the parcel located “beliggende i Øe i Husbye Sogn” (lying in Øe in Husby parish) — to Niels Jensen; and the deed to Thomas Jensen, signed on 18 December 1854 and registered on 4 April 1855. The farm the land came from can still be located in the landscape: in all likelihood it lay at what is now Bækbyvej 121 — registered in 1960 under the building name <t1>Øby</t1> — where the cadastral numbers still begin with the 13 of the main holding, and where the Building and Dwelling Register dates the present building to 1857, six years after the division. [S61, S62, S63]
3d950aa8361d: Aerial photograph from around 1950 of a four-winged thatched farm with an enclosed yard, surrounded by open fields
da7d6348116a: The farm on Bækbyvej, photographed from the air between 1948 and 1952, when Peter Højgaard was the owner — thatched ranges around an enclosed yard, with the fields drawn right up to the buildings. A later aerial photograph from 1960 (AAL_01734_14) records the same owner’s farm at Bækbyvej 121, cad. no. 13as, under the building name Øby. The property therefore lies on a later part of the main holding 13 from which the parcel in the marsh was separated in 1851.

7505a9a89673: The deed to Thomas Jensen describes what was sold as “et fritliggende Huus, der er beliggende i Silkjær og er Parcellen No. 2, Matr. No. 13b” — a detached house lying in Silkjær, being parcel no. 2, cad. no. 13b. The price was 240 rigsbankdaler, and with the purchase came the duty to bear his share of the aftægt — the retirement maintenance — owed to the old couple from the farm. Thomas Miltersen and Maren Madsdatter lived until 1864 and 1865, so for his first ten years on the place Thomas Jensen was obliged to help provide for the people from whose land it had been divided. The deed further stipulates that the property “maa ingenlunde mere anvendes til Brændeviinsbrænding eller til Drift af Brænderi” — may in no way any longer be used for distilling spirits or running a distillery. A corresponding clause stands in the next, unrelated deed in the same book, so the wording cannot be used as evidence that a distillery was ever run at Silkjær. [S63]
e42ad2f3ae83: The seller stayed on as a pensioner in the house he had just sold; the household at the census of 1 February 1855 is described in chapter 3. The family’s records put years to it: the seller was Niels Jensen Poulsgaard, born in Øe in 1802 and a widower since February 1851, when his wife Maren Jacobsdatter died; the stepdaughter Sidsel Cathrine Nielsdatter was her daughter from before the marriage, born in Møborg in 1820 — her father was Niels Christensen Roigård, hence the patronymic. The family were already people of the place: the census of 1850 lists the three together in a house in Øe — the rest of the entry is difficult to decipher. [S40, S60, S63]
b5bc2d97dc45: He had bought the parcel four months after he became a widower — and when he sold it again, both he and his stepdaughter stayed on. Against that background the transaction can be read as a provision for his old age: the house exchanged for maintenance and a roof over his wife’s daughter’s head. The prices — 200 rigsbankdaler in 1851 and 240 three years later, when the deed expressly mentions a house — can be read the same way: the modest rise may be connected with the seller’s continued residence and maintenance forming part of the bargain. But the deeds give reasons neither for the sale nor for the difference in price — the reading is an interpretation. [S40, S63]
913b17c3dba6: The dates fit into the family’s years: the deed was read on 4 April 1855, and on 9 July the same year Anne Marie Jansdatter gave birth to her son Niels. The deeds suggest the house may have been built during Niels Jensen’s short ownership. The deed of 1851 refers to the parcel with its appurtenances, crops and harvest, but mentions no buildings; the deed of 1854, by contrast, expressly mentions a detached house. That makes the years 1851—54 a likely possibility, but it does not prove the house was built precisely then. The parcel’s hartkorn land-tax assessment — 1 skæppe ¾ album, a little over an eighth of a tønde — shows a very small holding that could hardly feed a family on its own. Fishing was therefore not a sideline but a necessary part of the living; the census’s “han lever mest ved Fiskerie” — he lives mostly by fishing — says the same.
4cf3115265ca: Opening in the deed and mortgage book, pages 162—163, with the handwritten deed of 1854 and the marginal note on registration on 4 April 1855
cddcc7219def: The deed from Niels Jensen to Thomas Jensen of Husby, signed on 18 December 1854 — in the margin, the clerk’s note of registration on 4 April 1855. Here the property is described as a detached house “beliggende i Silkjær”, lying in Silkjær: the oldest dated record of the name.
fd6066237f91: Twenty-one years later the name had moved from the land to the man. When Thomas bought parcel 44b in Vedersø in 1876 and added it to the holding, the deed wrote him as <t1>“Thomas Jensen Silkjær”</t1> — the earliest known record of the name borne by a person, two years before the newspapers used it in the notice of his death. [S64]
f68aa2a26bf5: Opening in the deed and mortgage book of 1876 with document no. 247, registered 2 August 1876, the deed to cad. no. 44b in Vedersø
0a3bd6ba2e89: The deed and mortgage book, the opening with document no. 247, registered on 2 August 1876 — the deed to cad. no. 44b in Vedersø, where the buyer stands as “Thomas Jensen Silkjær”: the earliest known record of the name borne by a person.

de01021c43a9: After the wreck, an endorsement of allotment in January 1879 gave the son Niels Thomsen title to the property — the father’s estate, settled two months after the disaster. So 1878 was not a change of place but a change of generation. And on 21 November 1905 Niels received a name certificate entitling him to bear the name Niels Silkjær: the name of the place had become the family’s legal surname — endorsed in the margin beside his baptismal entry of 1855. [S61, S64, S65]
a11262a68aa5: The property grew and later passed on. Around 1917 land from cad. no. 78d was added, and on 24 May 1924 the whole was sold out of the family to J. F. Nielsen Lillevang. The land register carries the title on to Johannes Madsen in 1937 and Aksel Pedersen in 1952. [S61]

94febc4a472e: The parish registers’ “Økjær” covered more than one house. The registers place Thomas Jensen in Økjær, and in 1911 a woman from outside the family dies in the same place. The seller’s own family points the same way — and even shows the same double pattern: the census of 1850 lists Niels Jensen Poulsgaard, his wife and his stepdaughter in a house in Øe, but when his wife died in February 1851 — before the parcel in the marsh had been sold off — she was entered in Økjær, and the family file records both his death in 1862 and his stepdaughter’s in 1908 in the same place. The census says Øe, the parish register Økjær: the same pattern the family was later caught in. [S40, S60] The newspapers of 1878 put the byname “Ø.” after <t1>two</t1> other Husby men in the same boat — Thomas Jensen’s brother-in-law Anders Knudsen and his brother Esper Jensen (chapter 5) — while Iver Kristian Olesen, whom the family books place in Økjær, is there called Kløve. So Økjær held several households. For Esper Jensen the designations can be laid directly on top of one another: the newspapers call him Ø., the children in his household are born in Øe — and when he drowned in 1883, the parish register entered him as “2den Gang gift Huusmand, i Økjær og Fisker, født paa Husby Klit” — twice-married smallholder, in Økjær, and fisherman, born on Husby Klit. The same household, three designations. [S66] So Økjær was the name of an area and not of one building — which is why a family could sit on cad. no. 13b and still have “Økjær” written in the parish register.
0ba24aab0216: The geography fits. Økjær did not lie in the middle of a village but in the open country between Øby and Øhuse, where cad. no. 15 lay side by side with Silkjær’s no. 13 along the road that later became Øhusevej. The designation covered a farm, its smallholdings and the land around the low marsh — and the censuses’ “Øe” likewise covers both. The present property at Øhusevej 3 carries on the name Økjær and the cadastral number, but it is not the house the parish registers wrote about when they placed the family in Økjær.
4dd942af91bf: Two cadastral numbers through two hundred years
f718dcee2c67: The trail runs backwards: from today’s 15f and 13b back through the historical cadastral maps to the two main holdings they were divided from.
a1885f835319: Division has begun, but not in its present form
10d4b6129531: <t1>13b</t1> exists; the parcels around it lie differently
0f35853156cf: The maps, the censuses and the deeds meet in 13b: the maps take the number back to main holding 13, the deeds show the division in 1851, and the censuses place the family on it from 1890 — the land register from the allotment in 1879. The maps also settle that the two places were separate cadastral units all the way through, so the Silkjær property and the property associated today with Økjær lay on different numbers. What the maps do not show is the use of names: a main holding is not one house, and the area name Økjær lay across both.<t1>?</t1><n1/>
e5f0a7b664f9: The sequence in the table is based on the cadastral maps; ownership is recorded in the land register and the deeds: Thomas Jensen received the deed to 13b in 1854/55, and the title can be followed in the family until the sale in 1924.
a024af71776b: The use of names followed two layers. Økjær was the name of the area in the parish’s own language — the marsh and the houses around it, cad. no. 13b among them — and so the residence the priest wrote down. Silkjær was the property and later the man. On the lifeboat crew’s note of 1915, Silkjær is precisely the fixed point from which the neighbour gets his address. The name also appears in several spellings — Silkjær and Silkær — sometimes in the same document. And one entry shows the two names in the same line: at Thomas Nielsen Silkjær’s confirmation in Husby in 1896, the parish register lists the confirmand “af Økjær” (of Økjær) and his father as “Husmd. og Fisker Niels Thomsen (kaldt Silkjær)” — smallholder and fisherman Niels Thomsen (called Silkjær). The priest himself recorded that the man was officially called Thomsen but went by the name of the place, a decade before the name certificate. <t1>So the two designations appeared as two layers: Økjær was the address; Silkjær was the father’s byname.</t1> There is therefore no contradiction between the parish registers’ Økjær and the ownership of 13b. Where the boundary of the Økjær area ran is not known — but that does not change where the family lived. [S73]

d50f4c2cbec2: The Husby parish book has a biography for the farm — spelt <t1>Silkær</t1>. <t2>Johannes Madsen</t2>, born in Husby on 15 June 1891, married to Marie Jensen from Madum, seven children born between 1916 and 1933. And then the sentence that dates the change of ownership:
6ad01c494868: “Madsen bought the farm in 1936 with 17 tønder of land, cultivated and uncultivated, and planted.”
cadf584f7fdb: So from 1936 the Madsen family were on the farm — the deed was registered the following year — twenty-four years before the school photograph in which the farm name still clung to the parish’s way of speaking. Whom Johannes Madsen bought it from, the parish book does not say — the land register does: J. F. Nielsen Lillevang, who had taken over the property from the family in 1924. That the family who bore the name had owned the place for almost seventy years the book does not mention by a single word. Two cows, three head of cattle, fattening pigs, two horses, and thirty years of milk carting: that was what life on the place looked like, long after the name had travelled on without it.
d025b25b57fe: The sequence before 1936 is in the court books: the family itself from 1855 to 1924, then Lillevang. When Niels Thomsen took the farm’s name for himself, he was living on his father’s property.
82c789a5f3f5: A school photograph from Husby School in 1960 shows the farm name’s later life: a boy is noted as <t1>“Kurt Pedersen (Silkjær)”</t1>. His name was Pedersen; the parish identified him by the place, while another family owned the property. So the farm name was still in use as a place designation in 1960. The local history archive confirms that the custom was common in the district: people were called by the name of their farm, and with the Names Act of 1905 many officially took a surname after their farm — exactly the road Silkjær took in this family. [S115]
5a127c013c1c: <t1>Vort Sogns Historie</t1> (Our Parish’s History) for Husby parish contains 48 residents’ biographies, and Silkjær appears in two of them: Johannes Madsen’s entry on the farm itself (bought 1936) and Ole Lauridsen’s entry, in which his wife Ane Marie Nielsen Silkjær has her parents and grandparents listed. <t2>The sequence before 1936 is not in the book.</t2> The work was paid for by subscribers and includes only the places that bought space — and only the owner living on the place around 1950.
557d533cb599: The parish registers use <t1>Økjær</t1> consistently for the family’s home over forty years — as the name of an area, not as a cadastral address. The property that bears the name today lies on cad. no. 15, now 15f, and is linked to Thomas Jensen or Niels Thomsen neither in deeds nor in the land register; the family’s title concerns 13b. The picture of a consistent Økjær rests on six original entries. At Niels Thomsen’s baptism in 1855 the register gives his father as “Hmd. Øekjær Thomas Jensen”. In the register of deaths for 1863 the wife appears as “Huusm. i Øekjær Thomas Jensens Hustru” and the daughter Kjerstine as “Datter af ovennævnte huusmand i Øekjær Thomas Jensen … født i Øekjær”. In 1869 the daughter Karen Marie is “Datter af Hmd. i Økjær Thomas Jensen”. At Jesper Jensen’s death in 1883 he appears as a smallholder “i Økjær”, and at Thomas Nielsen Silkjær’s confirmation in 1896 the confirmand stands “af Økjær”, while his father is entered as “Niels Thomsen (kaldt Silkjær)”. So the designation stands in the originals throughout the period — in 1896 explicitly as an address beside the byname — and the register itself alternates between Øekjær and Økjær. [S38, S65, S66, S73]
f0358aa5e9ca: The sources thus document the course of ownership and naming for cad. no. 13b: Økjær was the area, Silkjær was the place and later the man. The confirmation entry of 1896 shows the two layers in the same line — the confirmand “af Økjær”, the father “kaldt Silkjær”. Still unresolved are the year the house was built, the age of the place name and the precise historical boundary of the Økjær area.
